body:
Meaning of living heritage

Food and clothing are among the most visible expressions of Indian cultural diversity. They reflect the natural environment, agricultural practices, occupations, religious beliefs, social customs and historical experiences of different communities.

Unlike historical monuments, which preserve physical evidence of the past, food and costume traditions continue through everyday activities. Families transmit culinary knowledge, methods of food preservation, weaving skills, embroidery designs and customs associated with clothing from one generation to another.

Living cultural heritage consists of inherited knowledge, skills, customs and practices that communities continue to practise, transmit and adapt.

A traditional garment is a tangible cultural object, but the knowledge required to weave, decorate and wear it forms part of intangible cultural heritage. Similarly, a prepared dish is a physical object, whereas its recipe, preparation methods and associated customs represent inherited cultural knowledge.

Factors shaping regional traditions

Climate and natural environment

Rainfall, temperature, soil, vegetation and access to water influence the availability of food and clothing materials. Rice and fish are important in many riverine and coastal regions, while drought-tolerant millets have traditionally been important in relatively dry regions.

Climate also influences clothing. Woollen garments help protect people from cold Himalayan winters, while lightweight cotton garments are suitable for many hot regions.

Occupation and livelihood

Agricultural communities develop food habits around locally cultivated crops. Fishing communities make use of marine and freshwater resources, while pastoral communities have traditionally relied on livestock for milk, dairy products and wool.

Occupations also influence clothing. Loose garments may facilitate physical work, while distinctive turbans, shawls and embroidered garments can express occupational or community identity.

Religion and social customs

Religious beliefs influence dietary preferences, fasting practices, food offerings and ceremonial meals. Clothing may also indicate participation in festivals, marriage ceremonies and other important stages of life.

These customs vary within religious and regional communities. The food habits of an entire population cannot be determined solely from its religion or geographical location.

Trade, migration and historical contact

Merchants, migrants, travellers and artisans introduce ingredients, garments and cultural practices into new regions. Consequently, regional traditions are not isolated or permanently fixed. They develop through interaction with neighbouring and distant societies.

Unity in diversity

India's culinary traditions display considerable variety despite sharing many basic ingredients. Rice, wheat, barley, millets, pulses and spices such as turmeric, cumin, ginger and cardamom are used across several regions. Different combinations and preparation methods produce distinctive local dishes.

Clothing follows a similar pattern. The sari is widely worn across India, but its fabric, weaving style, decoration and manner of draping vary considerably between regions and communities.

Thus, cultural unity does not require identical food or clothing. Shared cultural forms coexist with regional variation.

Prelims focus

  • Food and costume traditions are important expressions of living heritage.
  • The skills associated with cooking, weaving and embroidery constitute intangible cultural knowledge.
  • Ecology, occupation, religion, migration and trade influence regional traditions.
  • Shared ingredients and garment forms illustrate unity in diversity.
  • Trap: Geographical conditions influence cultural practices but do not determine them completely.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 8, Unity in Diversity, pp. 125–131; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts – II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 9, pp. 122 and 135; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9–12; GSSTB, Standard 7, Social Science, 2021 first edition, Chapter 8, Formation of Regional Culture. The project copies of the GCERT regional culture and human lifestyle extracts were unreadable; accessible textbook editions and official supplementary sources are used instead. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Food and Costume as Living Cultural Heritage

body:
Staple foods of India

A staple food is a food that forms a regular and substantial part of the customary diet of a population. Cereals, millets and pulses are important foundations of Indian food traditions.

The distribution of staple foods is closely related to agricultural conditions. However, irrigation, transport, trade and changing consumer preferences allow foods to become popular beyond their traditional cultivation areas.

Important grains and pulses

Food grainCommon Indian nameTraditional association
RiceChawalEastern, southern and coastal India
WheatGehunNorthern and northwestern plains
Pearl milletBajra or bajriDry regions of Rajasthan and Gujarat
SorghumJowar or juwarDeccan and western India
Finger milletRagi or nagliSouthern India and parts of tribal Gujarat
MaizeMakka or makaiParts of northern, western and tribal India
Pigeon peaTur or arharDal preparations across India
ChickpeaChanaPulses, gram flour and sattu

Relationship between ecology and diet

Wet plains and coastal regions

Rice cultivation is favoured by warm conditions and adequate water availability. River valleys, deltas and coastal plains have therefore developed extensive rice-based culinary traditions. Rivers, ponds and seas also provide fish and other aquatic foods.

Coconut is an important ingredient in many coastal cuisines, particularly along the western and southern coasts.

Arid and semi-arid regions

Low and uncertain rainfall makes drought-tolerant crops particularly valuable. Pearl millet is well adapted to relatively dry conditions and sandy soils. Sorghum and pulses also contribute to the food systems of many dry regions.

In Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat, traditional meals commonly include millet flatbreads, pulses and foods prepared from ingredients that can be stored for longer periods.

Mountain regions

Mountain environments contain considerable climatic variation. High-altitude cold regions favour hardy crops, while lower valleys may support rice, wheat, fruits and vegetables. Barley has traditionally been important in parts of the Himalayan region, especially Ladakh.

Pastoral regions

Pastoralism is a livelihood based primarily on the rearing of livestock. Milk, curd, buttermilk, butter and ghee have traditionally been important foods in pastoral and mixed agricultural-pastoral communities.

Traditional methods of preparing and preserving food

  • Steaming: Food is cooked using steam, as in idli and Gujarati dhokla.
  • Fermentation: Microorganisms transform food ingredients and may change their flavour, texture and acidity. Fermented rice-and-pulse batter is used in several Indian dishes.
  • Drying: Removing moisture helps preserve foods such as dried vegetables and grains for later use.
  • Pickling: Salt, oil, acidity or a combination of these helps preserve seasonal produce.
  • Roasting: Dry heat is used to prepare grains and other ingredients, including roasted gram used in sattu.

These practices help communities use seasonal resources, reduce dependence on immediately available fresh ingredients and develop distinctive culinary traditions.

Millets and pulses are different crop groups. Bajra, jowar and ragi are cereal grains belonging to the millet group, whereas tur, moong and chana are pulses.

Prelims focus

  • Bajra is pearl millet, jowar is sorghum and ragi is finger millet.
  • Nagli is a regional name for finger millet.
  • Rice-based diets are common in well-watered riverine and coastal regions.
  • Drought-tolerant millets are historically important in dry regions.
  • Trap: An important regional staple need not be cultivated or consumed exclusively in that region.

[References: NCERT, Class 10, Contemporary India – II, Chapter 4, Agriculture, pp. 36–40; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 8, pp. 127–128; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts – II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 9, p. 135; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, regional Food sections; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: The Dangs, Part A, Analytical Note, Major Characteristics of the District. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Traditional diets reflect locally available resources.

title: Staple Foods, Regional Ecology and Traditional Food Practices

body:
Northern Indian cuisine

The fertile plains of northern India support extensive cultivation of wheat, rice, pulses and other crops. Wheat-based flatbreads, lentils, seasonal vegetables and dairy products are important in several northern culinary traditions.

Punjab and Haryana

The agricultural and livestock-rearing traditions of Punjab and Haryana contribute to the widespread use of wheat, maize and dairy products.

Punjab is particularly associated with sarson da saag, prepared from mustard greens, and makki di roti, a maize flatbread. This combination is traditionally enjoyed during winter. Lassi, a curd-based beverage, is another familiar feature of Punjabi cuisine.

Kashmir

Kashmiri cuisine includes rice, meat preparations, vegetables, dried fruits and spices. Saffron is an important locally cultivated ingredient.

Wazwan is a traditional multi-course ceremonial feast, particularly associated with Kashmiri Muslim weddings and hospitality. It is known for its elaborate meat preparations.

Rogan josh is a meat curry, commonly prepared with mutton or lamb. Kahwa is a traditional green tea preparation flavoured with ingredients such as saffron, cardamom and almonds.

Uttar Pradesh and Awadh

The cuisine of Awadh, centred historically on Lucknow, developed under the patronage of its Nawabs. It is associated with kebabs, pulao, biryani and slow-cooked preparations. The term dum cooking refers to cooking food slowly in a closed vessel so that heat and steam help develop its flavour.

Western Indian cuisine

Rajasthan

Traditional Rajasthani cuisine reflects adaptation to arid and semi-arid conditions. Millets, pulses, wheat, dried ingredients and dairy products contribute to a variety of dishes.

The famous combination of dal, baati and churma includes cooked pulses, baked wheat-dough balls and a sweet preparation made from crushed cooked cereal dough.

Another important example is ker sangri. Ker is a desert shrub whose berries are used as food, while sangri refers to the edible pods of the khejri tree. These ingredients demonstrate how communities make culinary use of plants adapted to dry environments.

Maharashtra

Maharashtra contains both coastal and inland culinary regions. The Konkan coast is associated with rice, coconut and fish preparations, while jowar and bajra have traditionally been important in parts of the inland Deccan.

Bhakri is a flatbread that may be prepared from jowar, bajra or other grains. Puran poli is a sweet stuffed flatbread, commonly containing cooked pulses and jaggery or sugar. It is also prepared in neighbouring regions under different names and variations.

Goa

Goan cuisine reflects the coastal environment and historical Portuguese influence. Rice, fish and coconut are important ingredients in many local dishes.

Vindaloo illustrates Portuguese influence on Goan food through its historical association with a vinegar-based preparation. Bebinca is a traditional layered dessert associated with Goa.

Central Indian traditions

Central India has varied food traditions shaped by agriculture, forests and the customs of different communities. Wheat, rice, maize, millets and pulses are important ingredients.

Poha, made from flattened rice, is strongly associated with the breakfast traditions of Madhya Pradesh, especially Indore. Its popularity in neighbouring Maharashtra and other states also illustrates the movement of food traditions across regional boundaries.

Important regional associations

RegionFood traditionIdentifying feature
PunjabSarson da saag and makki di rotiMustard greens and maize
KashmirWazwanCeremonial multi-course feast
KashmirKahwaFlavoured green tea
AwadhDum preparationsSlow cooking in a closed vessel
RajasthanDal baati churmaPulses, baked bread and sweet preparation
RajasthanKer sangriDesert berries and khejri pods
MaharashtraBhakri and puran poliFlatbread traditions
GoaVindaloo and bebincaHistorical Portuguese influence
Madhya PradeshPohaFlattened rice

Prelims focus

  • Makki di roti is prepared from maize, not wheat.
  • Wazwan is associated with Kashmir and is a ceremonial feast rather than a single dish.
  • Ker sangri demonstrates adaptation to Rajasthan's dry environment.
  • Goan cuisine reflects coastal resources and Portuguese cultural contact.
  • Dum cooking is particularly associated with Awadhi culinary traditions.

[References: NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Goa and Madhya Pradesh regional Food sections; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, regional culinary profiles for North and West India, Rajasthan and Goa; NCERT, Class 10, Contemporary India – II, Chapter 4, Agriculture, pp. 36–40. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
